analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, towns, and co-ops offer broadband even where state laws ban it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2021, it picked up 18 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Roughly 18 states have laws that stop cities, counties, or cooperatives from building their own broadband networks. This bill would amend the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to bar states from prohibiting community broadband run by a city, a public-private partnership, or a cooperative. It also requires any government running a network to apply its rules to competing private providers without favoring itself, and keeps community networks subject to the same telecom laws as everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents in places private broadband companies haven't built or don't compete in — often rural areas and small towns — plus the cities, tribes, and co-ops that want to build networks themselves. Where a community network exists, residents often see a second internet option, which tends to lower prices and improve service.

how_it_helps.text: No state could prohibit a public provider, a public-private partnership, or a cooperatively organized provider from offering broadband, overriding state laws that currently ban community-built networks.
It gives local governments and tribes a federal right to fill gaps where private providers have declined to build, including tribal lands, which the bill expressly counts as state or local entities.

It keeps government-run networks on a level playing field: any city operating a network must apply its own ordinances and rules to competing private providers without discriminating in favor of itself, and community networks remain subject to all the same federal and state telecom rules as private providers.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies, which would face public or cooperative competitors in markets where state law currently shields them. Local taxpayers could also bear risk in towns where a community network is financed with public bonds and underperforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies

drawbacks.text: Municipal broadband projects can be expensive and risky; if a city builds a network that fails to attract enough subscribers, local taxpayers can be left covering the debt — the bill does not create any special review for that financial risk.
Incumbent providers argue that government-owned networks deter private investment in the same area, and the industry has long supported the state laws this bill would override.
The bill preempts state authority over local broadband decisions, which raises the same federalism objection Republicans and some state officials raise whenever Congress overrides state law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but conditional: community broadband works best where private providers have refused to build, and the bill includes guardrails — anti-discrimination rules and a savings clause keeping community networks under the same telecom laws as everyone else — that answer the fairness objections. The financial risk of failed municipal projects falls on local taxpayers, not the federal government, so the bill itself doesn't guarantee good projects, it only permits them.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its communications subcommittee for the entire Congress and was never scheduled for a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on March 8, 2021, joined by Reps. Golden, Neal, Pingree, Norton, and McGovern.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology.
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies come out ahead: the state laws that keep community-run networks out of their markets remain in force, and residents in areas without competition have no new option. The bill's 19 supporters gained nothing.

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Broadband Act and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Golden, Neal, Pingree, Norton, and McGovern
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Communications and Technology
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 9, 2021 and took no action on it.

against.name: Major cable and telephone broadband providers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Long supported the state laws barring municipal broadband that this bill would override, and opposed federal action to strike them down.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no Republican support before dying in committee.

industries.note: These companies benefit from state laws that bar cities, co-ops, and public-private partnerships from building competing networks. The bill would remove that shield, exposing them to public and cooperative competition in markets they have chosen not to serve or serve well.

industries.industry: Rural electric cooperatives and community co-ops
industries.note: Cooperatively organized providers are expressly covered by the bill, letting co-ops offer broadband where state law currently forbids it. Their gain — service to residents private providers skipped — runs directly alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Local governments and tribal nations considering public networks
industries.note: The bill would restore their legal ability to build or partner on broadband, though they would still bear the financing risk of any project they launch.
